1:
The three grammarians all unsettle the verse before expounding it. Ellicott reports that the external evidence is very strong for a different reading, with or for liberty did Christ make us free; stand fast, then, and be not entangled, and sees no sufficient reason why it should not be adopted; the best grammarians, he adds, take the phrase in the sense for liberty. Robertson agrees on the case, calling it dative rather than instrumental, for the freedom that belongs to us children of the freewoman. Barnes goes further than either and says the verse properly belongs to the previous chapter and should not have been separated from it.

On what the liberty consists of, Gill gives the fullest enumeration and guards every term of it: freedom from sin, not from its indwelling but from its dominion, guilt and damning power; from the captivity and tyranny of Satan, though not from his temptations and insults; from the ceremonial law as a handwriting of ordinances, a rigid severe schoolmaster and a middle wall of partition; from the moral law as a covenant of works and from its curse and condemnation and all expectation of life by the deeds of it, but expressly not from obedience to it as held forth by Christ and as a rule of walk. Wesley reads the liberty narrowly, from the ceremonial law. Henry takes it as enfranchisement, and adds the ground: we owe it to Christ, who by his merits satisfied the demands of the broken law and by his authority as a king discharged us from the carnal ordinances.

Calvin refuses to let it rest at ceremonies. That would be a small matter; this is but a stream which must be traced to a higher source, that Christ was made a curse to redeem us from the curse of the law, and rescued us from the tyranny of sin, Satan and death. Then he turns on his own critics. Many charge us with excessive zeal when they see us contending so warmly for freedom of faith against the tyranny of the Pope, and raise a prejudice among ignorant people as if the whole object of our pursuit were licentiousness. But the question is not whether you shall eat this food or that, or observe a particular day; it is what is necessary to salvation, the liberty of conscience placed before the tribunal of God. If men lay an unjust burden on our shoulders it may be borne; if they endeavour to bring our consciences into bondage, we must resist valiantly, even to death. Luther presses the verb instead, finding a vehemency in every word: stand, he says, as if to say that here is need of great diligence and vigilancy, for Satan most deadly hateth the light of the Gospel and stirs up storms and tempests as soon as it begins to appear, and they that are secure and negligent cannot keep this liberty. Not the liberty, he ends, wherewith the emperor hath made us free, but wherewith Christ hath made us free.

The word again is felt by two of them to need accounting for. Chrysostom takes it as the sting of the rebuke: by yoke Paul signifies the burdensomeness of the course, and by again their utter senselessness, since had they never experienced this burden they would not have deserved so severe a censure, but for those who by trial have learnt how irksome the yoke is to subject themselves to it once more is justly unpardonable. Calvin raises the difficulty the others pass over, that the Galatians had never lived under the law at all, and answers that it means only that they were not to be entangled as if they had never been redeemed, since apart from Christ neither Jew nor Gentile enjoys any freedom.
2:
The solemnity of the opening is remarked by everyone. Barnes unpacks who it is that speaks: the man who first preached the gospel to them, who had himself been circumcised, who was formerly a strenuous asserter of the necessity of observing the laws of Moses, and who is at this moment charged with still preaching circumcision. Ellicott hears the strong personality of the Apostle asserting itself, since instead of going into an elaborate proof he speaks with dogmatic authority as though his bare word were enough. Robertson notes that the conditional is of the third class, a supposable case but with terrible consequences, and that the pronoun asserts all his personal and apostolic authority. Gill catches the same weight in the next verse, calling its formula the form of an oath, a swearing by the living God.

Luther makes the verse a measuring instrument. Paul, he says, wonderfully stirred up with zeal and fervency of spirit, thundereth against the law and circumcision, and these thunderings the Holy Ghost wresteth from him. Then the use: this place is as it were a touchstone, whereby we may most certainly and freely judge of all doctrines, works, religions and ceremonies of all men. Whosoever teaches that anything besides faith in Christ is necessary to salvation, or devises any work or tradition by which forgiveness and everlasting life are supposedly obtained, hears in this place the sentence of the Holy Ghost pronounced against him. And the argument from the greater: seeing Paul durst give this sentence against the law and circumcision, which were ordained of God himself, what durst he not do against the chaff and the dross of men's traditions?

The obvious objection is raised by two of them and answered by one. Barnes will not let the statement be taken absolutely, since Paul had himself procured the circumcision of Timothy, and holds that where it is done for prudential considerations, so as not needlessly to irritate the Jews, nothing here touches it. Calvin presses the difficulty harder — did circumcision not profit Abraham, and will it not follow that none of the fathers were saved? — and answers it by a distinction he says runs through Paul: circumcision is viewed in two different aspects, in one place as a seal of the righteousness of faith, and here in contrast with Christ and faith and grace, viewed simply as a legal covenant founded on the merit of works. What the false apostles did was not to deny Christ but to make such a division between his grace and the works of the law as to leave not more than the half of salvation due to him; and Christ cannot be divided in this way. Whoever wishes to have the half of Christ, loses the whole. Barnes puts the same thing in his own idiom, that Christ is to be a whole Saviour and no rite is to divide the honour with his death.

On the debtor, the sharpest formulation is Ellicott's: he who allows himself to be circumcised commits himself wholly to the Law, just as he who is baptised commits himself wholly to Christ, and from that time forward he could not choose one part and refuse another. Clarke says the same more plainly, that he lays himself under obligation to fulfil all its precepts and ordinances. Robertson glosses the noun as one who has assumed an obligation and adds four words of his own: he takes the curse on himself. Luther turns the obligation into a futility — the more ye go about to satisfy the law and to be set free from it, the more ye entangle and snare yourselves in the yoke thereof, which is to go backward like the crab, and to wash away filth with filth. Wesley alone narrows the address, taking every man to mean every Gentile.
4:
Falling from grace is the sharpest division in the chapter, and the readings do not reduce to two. Clarke takes it at full weight: they had been brought into the grace of the Gospel, and by readopting the Mosaic ordinances they had apostatized from it and lost the grace communicated to their souls, by which they were preserved in salvation — and will not close the case, since whether some of them ever rose again is more than we can tell. Barnes empties the sentence of any such history, observing that the apostle does not say this had in fact ever occurred but merely makes a supposition. Ellicott relocates the term instead of weakening it: grace here is not a state or disposition in the believer but a divine act or relation, so that what is lost is a standing: the man who seeks justification another way is unchristianised, his relations to Christ cancelled. Robertson keeps the aorist blunt — ye left the sphere of grace in Christ and took your stand in the sphere of law — then fences it: Paul is not speaking of occasional sins, but of substituting law for Christ as the agent in salvation.

What made the fall was, all of them agree, a mixture rather than a denial. Calvin insists they were not so grossly mistaken as to believe they were justified by the law alone, but attempted to mix Christ with the law, and concludes that the smallest part of justification cannot be attributed to the law without renouncing Christ altogether. Clarke states the alternative with no middle term: you must have the law and no Christ, or Christ and no law. Gill notices that the Greek can be turned about, either that the Galatians are abolished from Christ or, by a figure, that Christ is abolished unto them. Wesley reads the loss covenantally, that they disclaim the benefit of this gracious dispensation.

On the hope of righteousness the interest shifts to what is future in it. Barnes cautions that the main idea is not waiting as though the thing were delayed but expecting. Ellicott builds a whole scheme on the phrase: the righteousness conferred at baptism is only a sort of ideal or potential righteousness, inherent in the kingdom the Christian has entered rather than in the Christian himself, and made actual only at the end of his career. Clarke goes to the verb and dissects it into its three particles to yield we receive out of it, no fanciful derivation but one that exists in the experience of every genuine Christian, who continually receives foretastes of a glory whose fulness he expects after death. Calvin uses the verse to level the fathers with us, since their faith was the same but concealed by the veil of ceremonies, which is why Paul distinguishes us from them by the word Spirit. Luther observes that hope in Scripture means both the thing hoped for and the affection of the one hoping, so that the clause yields a double sense.

Faith working by love draws the warmest writing. Clarke calls this humble, holy, operative, obedient love the grand touchstone of all human creeds and confessions, since faith without it has neither soul nor operation and is, in James's language, dead. Barnes turns the point against a kind of religion: mere orthodoxy, however bold and self-confident and sound, may not be inconsistent with contentions and strifes and logomachies and divisions. Ellicott divides the labour neatly — faith makes a man seek to do the will of Christ, love tells him what that will is — and says the faith so described is in no conflict with James. Robertson notes the middle voice and borrows Burton's phrase, the moral dynamic. Calvin adds the historical guard, that circumcision is not pronounced always useless but abolished since Christ came,.
7:
The three grammarians take the verb for hindering three different ways,. Barnes reports Doddridge's, that it is an Olympic expression properly signifying coming across the course while a man is running in it, so as to jostle him out of the way. Ellicott says the metaphor is not quite the same and goes behind it to the root, whose original meaning is to break up a road, as an army does before advancing forces. Robertson finds a homelier equivalent: to cut in on one, for all the world like our use of one cutting in on us at the telephone. He weighs the singular pronoun and concludes there was some ringleader in the business. Clarke fixes responsibility the other way: they could only be turned aside by their own consent. Calvin notices the rhetoric rather than the metaphor: the censure is deliberately mingled with approbation of their former course so that, brought to a sense of shame, they may return the faster, the astonishment in the question being intended to produce a blush.

On the persuasion's source, Calvin observes that Paul does not say plainly that it is not from God but reaches it by circumlocution: God is never inconsistent with himself, and he it is who by my preaching called you, so this new persuasion has come from some other quarter. Luther takes the verse out of its controversy altogether and makes it a rule for the afflicted conscience. The devil, he says, is a marvellous persuader, and knows how to amplify the least sin, yea a very trifle, so that the tempted man shall think it a most heinous crime worthy of eternal damnation; and the troubled conscience is to be raised up as Paul raised the Galatians, by being told that this persuasion cometh not of Christ.

Whether the leaven is bad doctrine or bad men is disputed flatly. Calvin says it refers, he thinks, to doctrine and not to men, and describes Satan's stratagem as never an avowed destruction of the gospel but a tainting of its purity by false opinions, which many therefore resist less determinedly. Ellicott says it seems decidedly more in accordance with the context to take the little leaven as referring rather to a few seceders than to a little bad doctrine. Barnes canvasses three possibilities and settles on the false teachers; Wesley agrees in five words, that one troubler troubles all. Robertson cautions against pressing the figure at all, since it is merely the pervasive power of leaven that the proverb involves, not leaven as a symbol of evil. Clarke concedes the objection before answering it: granted that circumcision is in itself a small matter, yet since every man circumcised is a debtor to the whole law, it leads necessarily to total perversion.

The confidence of the tenth verse raises a scruple that Luther and Gill meet independently and in the same terms — that Scripture forbids trust to be put in men. Both answer by dividing the object: faith trusts God and cannot be deceived, charity believes man and is often deceived, and Gill adds that this is the love which hopes all things. Luther defends the second as indispensable — if one man should not believe another, what life should we live upon earth? Calvin hears in the added words a reminder that repentance is a heavenly gift which they must ask from God. On the troubler the grammarians will not be drawn: Robertson thinks it unlikely Paul knew precisely who the leader was, and Ellicott that he fixes on no particular person but says that whoever he may be God will judge him — adding that judgment here is not condemnation but being put upon trial. Wesley alone is confident it was one person chiefly. Henry draws the pastoral rule, that in reproving sin and error we should always distinguish between the leaders and the led.
11:
Paul is answering a charge, and the commentators agree on where it came from. Robertson states it baldly: some of the Judaizers circulated the slander that Paul preached circumcision, to ruin his influence. Gill, Clarke and Barnes all trace the handle for it to the circumcising of Timothy, Gill adding that he did that as a thing indifferent, for the sake of the Jews, and never preached it as necessary to salvation. Ellicott is the one who will not let the charge be wholly groundless. We should naturally infer, he says, that the Apostle had at one time seemed to preach, or at least to permit, circumcision, and that time and events deepened his conviction of the radical antagonism between ceremonial Judaism and Christianity, so that he feels himself open to a charge of something like inconsistency. Calvin is interested in the form of the argument, calling it an argument from the final cause and asking whether it proves anything: it would be wholly in Paul's power to avoid every danger were he only to mix ceremonies with Christ, and though sincerity does not by itself establish a doctrine, no man would be so mad as to bring distress on himself of his own accord. He then lays on the false apostles the suspicion that in preaching circumcision they consulted their own ease rather than faithfulness to Christ.

On why the cross gives offence, Clarke reasons from consistency: were he a friend to circumcision he must soon cease to preach Christ crucified, and the Jews would be his enemies no longer. Wesley locates the offence in what the preaching implied, the abolition of the law, and draws the line he thinks Paul draws — that he did not condemn conforming out of condescension to anyone's weakness, even to the ceremonial law, but absolutely condemned those who taught it as necessary to justification.

The wish of the twelfth verse splits them three ways. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley read it as excommunication, Clarke supporting this from Kypke's examples of the verb for cutting off from society or office, and answering the objection that Paul could have excommunicated them himself by pleading that his authority in Galatia was too weakened to exercise any ecclesiastical function. Gill and Calvin read it as a prayer for destruction, Gill glossing it as being cut off out of the land of the living by the immediate hand of God. Ellicott and Robertson read it as self-mutilation, and Ellicott gives the case: the ancient Greek interpreters and a large majority of moderns take it so, the Galatians being familiar with the practice from the priests of Cybele, whose worship centred in their country; let them carry it further and not stop at circumcision. Barnes knows the reading, calls it singular and monstrous, records with amazement that a standard lexicon has adopted it,.

Whether such a wish is lawful at all is faced squarely by two. Calvin puts the objection himself — how is this reconciled with the mildness of an apostle, who ought to wish that all should be saved? — and concedes its force so far as men are concerned, since God wills that we seek the salvation of all men without exception, as Christ suffered for the sins of the whole world; but devout minds are sometimes carried beyond men to fix their eye on God's glory, and would rather the whole world perished than the smallest portion of it were withdrawn. Luther asks the same question more briskly and answers by a rule: cursing is lawful not always nor for every cause, but when God's word is blasphemed, then whatsoever is without God and his word, accursed be it, though it be an apostle or an angel from heaven. Ellicott alone declines to defend the verse, allowing that at best such words fall some way short of the meekness and gentleness of Christ.
13:
Calvin opens with a distinction he says he has made before: liberty is one thing and the use of it another. Liberty lies in the conscience and looks to God; the use of it lies in outward matters and deals not with God only but with men. The question, he insists, is not in what manner we are free before God but how we may use our liberty among men: a good conscience submits to no slavery, yet to practise outward slavery, or to abstain from using liberty, is attended by no danger. Clarke draws the same boundary with a harder edge: your liberty is from what would oppress the spirit, not from what would restrain the flesh; the Gospel proclaims liberty from the ceremonial law but binds you faster under the moral law, and to pretend freedom from the moral law is Antinomianism. Henry states the principle plainly, that though Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law he has not freed us from the obligation of it.

The grammarians work on the sentence itself. Barnes observes that the word use, supplied by the translators, obscures the sense: the point is not freedom from virtuous restraints but from the servitude of sin and of ceremonies. Robertson agrees there is no word for it in the Greek and would supply a verb of turning: turn not your liberty into a spring-board for license. Ellicott finds a stress on the verb serve: the Apostle has dissuaded them from every other servitude, and this one he will permit. Ellicott also guesses at history, that sensual excess was the especial danger of the Gentile churches such as Corinth, and that the fickle Galatian character made the caution worth hinting even where the pressure was Judaising. Clarke notes that several excellent manuscripts and versions read not by love but in the love of the Spirit serve one another.

The quotation of Leviticus 19:18 raises a difficulty that only Calvin states openly. The law consists of two tables, the first on the worship of God and the second on the love of our neighbour; how then can all its precepts be included under the second, when it is ridiculous to make a part the same as the whole? He records the usual escape — that the first table contains nothing more than to love God with the whole heart — and rejects it, since Paul expressly names love to our neighbour, so a more satisfactory solution must be sought. His own is that piety does rank higher and the first table is more valuable in God's sight, but God being invisible, piety is hidden from the eyes of men, and ceremonies are no certain proof of it; love of the neighbour is what can be seen. Gill and Wesley take precisely the road Calvin refuses, both arguing that the second commandment implies the first — Gill because the love of God is the cause and therefore the evidence of love to the neighbour, Wesley because none can love his neighbour without loving God.

Two further notes are worth keeping. Robertson calls the verse a striking paradox, since Paul is urging obedience to the very law he has been arguing against, and answers that this is the moral law adduced as proof of the new love and life. Ellicott observes that in the original command neighbour appears to mean a fellow Israelite, that our Lord widened it in the parable of the Good Samaritan, and that the wider sense is used here; Robertson notes the same restriction. Barnes admires the transition itself, that Paul changes with great skill from doctrinal argument to practical remark. Luther puts it architecturally: having laid the foundation, Paul now builds gold, silver and precious stones upon it — good works indeed, beside which the vain work of ceremonies is far inferior.
15:
On the biting and devouring, the observations are mostly on the figure. Gill notes what Paul does not say: not that grievous wolves had entered the flock, but that the sheep were acting the part of wolves to one another, which is unnatural. Robertson recalls the famous story of two snakes that seized each other by the tail and each swallowed the other. Luther supplies the historical evidence, that when Africa was perverted by the Manichees the Donatists followed, one sect bringing forth another and each condemning the rest. Clarke and Barnes draw the practical moral: nothing is so destructive to the peace of the soul as religious disputes, and the readiest way to destroy a church's spirituality is to excite a spirit of contention. Calvin alone proposes a cause behind the effect: the false doctrine was probably itself a judgment from heaven upon their pride, as Deuteronomy 13:3 warns that God proves his people by such a prophet.

Whether the sixteenth verse is a promise or a command divides the grammarians from the translators. Barnes reports that the margin and Tindale render it as an imperative, fulfil not, but prefers the common rendering as the more significant. Robertson makes it a plain future on the strength of the double negative — not ye shall not but ye will not. Ellicott establishes only that the Spirit here is undoubtedly the Holy Spirit, not the spirit in man. Calvin hears an accusation in the exhortation, that the Galatians are indirectly told they are carnal and destitute of the Spirit, since whence did their violence toward each other proceed but from the lust of the flesh? Clarke reads it as recovery rather than progress: get back the Spirit you have grieved and lost. Luther uses the verse against the schoolmen, who reasoned that if love fulfils the law then love is righteousness and the law justifies — a foolish consequence, drawn from precept to work, as though the law commanding love produced the work of love out of hand.

The seventeenth verse is where the readings part most sharply, and the question is what the frustrated will is willing. Barnes objects that cannot do is far stronger than the original and doubts the Greek will bear it, preferring so that ye do not the things that ye would. Ellicott and Henry both take the thwarted desire to be the good one, Henry adding that the corrupt nature which remains shall nevertheless not have dominion. Wesley reverses the referent outright: the things ye would are what the flesh would, and the Spirit's strengthening is precisely what prevents them. Clarke draws his own conclusion from the deadlock and puts it as a question — who can suppose that Paul speaks this of adult Christians? Robertson keeps the image martial, a spiritual duel, and rejects Lightfoot's claim that the verb for longing cannot be used of the Spirit, since it means simply to long for, as Christ and Satan both long for the city of Man Soul.

Ellicott adds that this antithesis is not dualism, since nothing shows Paul considered matter itself evil; the body becomes the seat of evil, and the flesh is the body as animated by an evil principle. Calvin refuses the narrower sense too, saying flesh denotes the whole nature of man and not merely the lower senses, and asks where then we shall find a drop of goodness in free will. On the last verse Ellicott makes flesh and law correlative, so that freedom from the one is freedom from the other, law being the standard unaided nature strives in vain to fulfil; Robertson notes that Paul writes under law where one might expect under the flesh, the two being one in result. Calvin turns it to comfort, that duties are accepted despite their defects and the law now acts only as a kind adviser.
19:
Both grammarians sort the catalogue into four groups, and neither the same way. Ellicott's are sins of sensuality, of superstition, of temper, and excesses, and he passes on a theory that all sinfulness resolves into two elementary instincts, self-preservation and reproduction. Robertson's are sensual sins, idolatry with witchcraft, eight words for sins of the spirit in personal relations, then excess; he adds that ancient writers were fond of such lists and that this deadly one runs past seven. Wesley notices what neither does, that the works are plural because they are distinct from and often inconsistent with each other, whereas the fruit of the Spirit is singular, being all consistent and connected; and he holds that Paul selected the vices to which the Galatians were most inclined and the graces they most needed. Gill, Barnes and Wesley take the list as proof that flesh cannot mean the body, since wrath, strife and envyings have no seat there; Barnes asks whether a nature producing this can be regarded as pure.

Three of the words are textually doubtful and the doubts are recorded. Clarke and Ellicott agree that adultery is wanting in the best manuscripts. On murders Ellicott notes its absence from the two oldest and says internal considerations tell either way; Clarke, who also finds it missing in several, conjectures that similarity of sound to the word before it suggested it here. Ellicott adds that singular and plural are strangely mixed through the list, that wrath should be wraths, and that strife is a mistake in the Authorised version.

Witchcraft produces the sharpest exchange. Barnes traces the Greek word from the giving of medicine, through poisoning, to magic art, since in savage nations medicine consisted much in incantations — then withholds assent: the apostle does not vouch for the actual existence of witchcraft, but says what was known as such was itself a proof of man's corrupt nature, a systematised attempt to impose on mankind. Wesley will have none of that. It means witchcraft strictly speaking and not poisoning, he argues, from its being joined with the worship of devil-gods rather than with murder; and since the thing is frequently and solemnly forbidden in the Old Testament, to deny that there is or ever was any such thing is by plain consequence to deny the authority of both Testaments. Clarke stays with the etymology, deriving the root either from bringing ease or from bringing pain, since the same drugs served to restore health or destroy an enemy, to procure love or produce hatred. Ellicott supplies the local colour, that such practices were especially common in Asia Minor, the burning of the books at Ephesus being evidence.

The threatening at the end raises the objection Calvin states for his opponents: in this way all are cut off from hope, for who is not chargeable with some of these sins? He answers that Paul threatens not all who have sinned but all who remain impenitent, since the saints themselves fall and return. Robertson reaches the same conclusion from the verb, which is the one for habitual practice and not for occasional doing, so the habit is what proves a man outside the kingdom. Cyril arrives from a third direction, insisting on the tense of the apostle's own parallel — he said not such are some of you but such were some of you — and concluding that sin committed in ignorance is pardoned while persistent wickedness is condemned. Luther aims the sentence at the heretics, puffed up with imagined spiritual attainments while securely performing the works of the flesh, and hopes some may be terrified into fighting them. Calvin adds that Paul glances at the false apostles, who laid aside far more valuable instruction to dispute about ceremonies. Clarke, on emulations, gives his own example of zeal pursued by cruel means: inquisitions supporting true religion by burning alive those who profess it.
22:
That Paul writes fruit where he wrote works is pressed by nearly everyone and denied by one. Barnes says the change is not without design, since these things do not flow from our own nature, and Paul refuses to trace them to our hearts even when renewed. Robertson calls it a shift of figure to the normal out-cropping of the Spirit in us, a beautiful tree with nine luscious fruits on it. Gill grounds the metaphor in dependence: they are owing to divine bounty as the fruits of the earth are, not to a man's self. Calvin quotes an epigram to the same effect: where the flesh rules the work exceeds the fruit, and so, without even mentioning the work, this is called the fruit of the Spirit. Ellicott alone will not have it: there does not seem to him to be any essential difference between this term and the one used above.

What the list is worth beside the moral philosophy of the ancients interests two of them. Robertson makes the comparison specific, judging Paul's list better than the four cardinal virtues of the Stoics: temperance is alike in both, but kindness is better than justice. Calvin concedes more to the pagans than either and then takes it back. There have often appeared in unrenewed men remarkable instances of gentleness, integrity and generosity, he grants, and names them — Curius and Fabricius for courage, Cato for temperance, Scipio for kindness, Fabius for patience — but it was only in the sight of men and as members of civil society that they were so distinguished, and all were specious disguises, since nothing is pure in God's sight but what proceeds from his Spirit.

On the individual graces the notes are mostly lexical, with one dispute. Ellicott raises it: it may be questioned whether peace here is the tranquillity shed abroad in the heart by reconciliation with God, or rather, from the context, peaceableness towards men — and Barnes takes without hesitation the sense Ellicott doubts. On love standing first, Luther says it had been enough to have said love and no more, since love extends itself to all the other fruits, and that Paul set it first to admonish Christians that before all things they should love one another; Wesley calls it the root of all the rest, and Ellicott the moving principle in which Christianity is not perhaps alone, but alone in the consistency with which it carries it out. Barnes gives temperance a long note to reclaim it, since we now use the English word in a much narrower sense, of abstinence from strong drink, whereas the Greek denotes self-rule over every evil propensity. Cyril, closing a lecture, prays that the Spirit be sent so his hearers may render up these fruits, and recites all nine in order.

The last clause divides them by depth. Clarke takes it at face value: lives adorned by these virtues cannot be condemned by any law. Ellicott corrects a grammatical mistake first, that it means against such things and not, as many older commentators understood, against such men, and adds that these graces are above law as well as beyond it, since a ruder system of commands sanctioned by punishment could not produce them. Calvin dismisses the obvious reading — that the law is not directed against good works — as too shallow, and finds a deeper meaning, that where the Spirit reigns the law has no dominion: it continues to teach and exhort, but our subjection to it is withdrawn by the Spirit of adoption. He then turns it into a taunt, that the false apostles who enforced subjection to the law were no less eager to escape its yoke. Luther says the same thing from the other side: there is indeed a law, but not against such, for the righteous man does without constraint what the law requires.
24:
Why Paul says crucified rather than merely killed is answered by Ellicott and Robertson in the same direction. Ellicott argues from the shape of the relation: its central point is the crucifixion, and the Christian is bound to make his Master's death his own so far as sin is concerned, so the flesh is not killed but crucified — and he dates the act, strictly, to baptism. Robertson makes it a definite past event by the tense and finds in the preposition an emphasis on the completeness of the extermination, borrowing Burton's definition of the flesh as the force in men that makes for evil. Calvin uses the word to locate the agency elsewhere: it shows that the mortification of the flesh is the effect of the cross of Christ, and this work does not belong to man.

How complete the crucifixion is they then answer differently. Barnes takes it at its strongest, that the corrupt passions are as though dead and have no power over us; Ellicott likewise says the Christian will not need to be taught peaceableness or self-control, because the contrary impulses were killed at the moment he gave himself wholly to a crucified Saviour; and Clarke draws the boldest inference of the chapter, that God has fully designed to save all who believe from all sin, inward and outward. Calvin will not go so far, holding that the flesh is not yet entirely destroyed but has no right to exercise dominion and ought to yield. Luther is franker still: the saints, not having utterly put off the sinful flesh, neither fear nor love God as perfectly as they ought, and are provoked to anger, envy and impatience, which nevertheless they do not accomplish. Wesley finds a middle term in the figure itself, that the flesh is nailed to a cross whence it has no power to break loose but is continually weaker and weaker. Gill guards the subject rather than the predicate: the elect not yet called are secretly Christ's but cannot have this said of them, so those openly his are meant.

On living and walking by the Spirit, Calvin supplies the analogy the sentence needs: as the soul does not remain idle in the body but gives motion and vigour to every member, so the Spirit cannot dwell in us without manifesting himself in outward effects — and he notes that many are daring enough to boast falsely of living in the Spirit, whom the apostle here challenges to a proof of the fact. Ellicott offers two constructions, if we live by the Spirit, deriving our life from him, or if we live to the spirit on the analogy of living unto the Lord, and observes that the life the Spirit quickens still needs human co-operation. Robertson notes that the verb is not the one used earlier for walking, and renders it: let us make our steps by the help and guidance of the Spirit.

Vainglory is traced to a root by both the men who take it seriously. Calvin calls ambition the mother of many evils in society and particularly in the church, defines the word as the desire of honour by which every one wishes to excel all others, and adds that provoking and envying are the daughters of ambition, since he who aspires to the highest rank must envy all others. Luther traces it to pride, which he says is the head-spring of all sin and confusion, and then makes a distinction the others do not: he who praises a man as a man is a liar, but when our ministry is praised we must endeavour to the uttermost that men magnify it, since that turns to their salvation. Wesley states the double motion in one line, provoking those beneath us and envying those above. Clarke alone declines to guess what occasioned it, saying plainly that we cannot tell.
